b: When “Yellowjackets” premiered over five years ago, it felt like a breath of fresh air in a television landscape that felt desolate amid the COVID-19 pandemic. A series following a high school girls’ soccer team whose lives are upended when their plane crashes in the Canadian wilderness felt unlike anything currently airing at the time, and before it. It really excelled in blending two timelines: the team post-crash in the 1990s and the survivors in the present day. Yet as the series progressed, these timelines began to feel at war with one another, and season by season the show lost its grasp on audiences and critics alike.

In its final season, the series has thankfully given the ‘90s timeline the screen time and respect it deserves. Season 4 begins with the survivors being evaluated in the hospital, after Natalie’s (Sophie Thatcher) distress signal went through and the crew was eventually saved. They look at showers like novelties, and their reflections in bathroom mirrors startle them as if they’re seeing ghosts. Propelled by Kurt Cobain’s crooning voice singing Nirvana’s “Where Did You Sleep Last Night,” the series finally seems ready to confront how the people who made it back adapted to no longer being forced to hunt each other for food, and for sport.

Each episode focuses on one of the surviving members attempting to re-integrate into society, forcing its actors to finally chew on material that rivals anything they’ve been given in the last two middling seasons. Lottie (Courtney Eaton) and Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) shut themselves off from their families; Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown) and Misty (Sammi Hanratty) attempt to find some normalcy; Akilah (Nia Sondaya) struggles to keep the team’s secrets; and Travis (Kevin Alves), Van (Liv Hewson), Melissa (Jenna Burgess), and Natalie are suspended in limbo, haunting the town of Wiskayok like ghosts of their former selves. Watching each of these characters attempt to mold themselves back into the teenagers they were before the crash is the most enjoyable “Yellowjackets” has been in years. It’s a shame that it doesn’t last long.

The newfound life injected into the series with the post-rescue timeline is smothered each time we’re forced to flip back to the present, where each plotline continues to feel like a baffling joke the writers aren’t necessarily in on. Here, the older versions of Taissa (Tawny Cypress) and Misty (Christina Ricci) desperately hatch a plan to eliminate Shauna (Melanie Lynskey), whose violent nature explodes under the weight of her crumbling family life.

But when Melissa (Hilary Swank) moves her family into the house beside her former lover, each woman begins to realize there’s no one from their past they can trust, despite the promises they’ve made and the plans they’ve already set in motion. While Cypress manages to leave this final season mostly unscathed, nothing is more interesting than watching the stunted adult versions of these characters chase each other around New Jersey.

In the present day, each act that should instill some sense of danger in the viewer is underscored by a trite score, unlike the unsettling chants and gasps woven into the orchestra in the ’90s timeline. Every creative choice, whether it be the music or the muted cinematography, feels like it’s been crafted to undersell the intrigue that should be present in a timeline rife with versions of these women whose minds have fractured even more as the decades have gone by. The meticulously crafted lives of each of these women have unraveled over the course of the series, but instead of sincerely engaging with the fallout, the series is more interested in having them act like caricatures of the women we were introduced to in Season 1. This is a disservice not only to the show, but to the actresses who helm it.
L-R: Tawny Cypress as Taissa and Melanie Lynskey as Shauna in Yellowjackets, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Darko Sikman/Paramount+.

The final season of “Yellowjackets” technically never takes its foot off the gas, forcing its audience to witness the horrors that took place between Natalie’s distress call and the team being rescued, how they fared back home, and, of course, how they exist decades later. But, by splitting this already jumbled series into three separate timelines, the series bloats itself beyond repair. By the end, I found myself wishing that this journey would halt altogether.

It’s frustrating, because the new sections wherein the survivors reel from the horrific acts of violence they saw and committed are undeniably a series-best effort. When the team makes it out of the wilderness, they’re forced to operate within a world that has changed in their absence. That’s also true for how the adult counterparts exist within the realm of this series, which at every turn feels desperate to boil down these fascinating characters until they become husks of the inherently flawed people we’re only allowed to witness in flashbacks.

While the series has shifted over its four seasons, each episode still begins with the crackle of an old television screen and the lyrics of the title track “No Return,” hauntingly performed by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker. It’s a title sequence that, in the years since the series’ premiere, has been hard to skip. The same cannot be said for the images that follow, which, no matter how hard this series tries, never manage to emulate the grit, guts, and glory in this carefully crafted opening.
Eight episodes were screened for review. Premieres on Showtime and Paramount+ November 20.
